summary: Describes a pseudowire encapsulation for TDM bit-streams such as T1, E1, T3 and E3 that ignores any structure the standard TDM framing imposes on the stream. This lets old telephone-style circuits be carried across packet networks. It is a standards-track document.

plainLanguage.summary: SAToP carries an old-style telephone line across a packet network. Each end takes the continuous bit stream, cuts it into fixed-size pieces, puts a small header on each piece and sends it as a packet. The network never looks inside the stream, so the line behaves like a line, but any packet loss reaches the customer interface.

questions: how does satop carry t1 and e1
subtitle: Carrying an old-style telephone bit stream across a packet network without looking inside it.

tldr.problem: Telephone networks hand over fixed-rate bit streams such as E1 and T1, and a service provider often has to carry them across an IP network that works in packets.
tldr.mechanism: SAToP is a pseudowire encapsulation: an interworking function at each end cuts the bit stream into fixed-size chunks, wraps each one in a 4-byte control word and an optional RTP header, and sends it as an ordinary packet.
tldr.outcome: The packet network carries the circuit without interpreting it, so any TDM signalling inside the stream survives, at the cost of exposing the customer interface to packet loss.

facts.label: Required payload sizes
facts.value: E1 256 bytes, T1 192 bytes, E3 and T3 1024 bytes

today: RFC 4553 is a Proposed Standard. It has not been obsoleted or updated, and the document itself describes no later revision of the encapsulation.

sections.title: What SAToP Carries
sections.content:
SAToP is an encapsulation layer for carrying Time Division Multiplexing (TDM) bit-streams over packet-switching networks. The bit-streams it covers are E1, T1, E3 and T3, the four line types named in ITU-T G.702. What makes it structure-agnostic is that the protocol ignores any structure the standard TDM framing imposes on the stream: the bits are moved across the network without being parsed, framed or interpreted. The same emulation is called emulation of unstructured TDM circuits in RFC 4197.

The approach suits deployments where the provider edge devices have no reason to interpret the TDM data or to take part in the TDM signalling. The stream is simply moved. SAToP follows the PWE3 pseudowire architecture of RFC 3985 and satisfies the general requirements of RFC 3916 and the requirements for unstructured TDM signals in RFC 4197.

A SAToP pseudowire may be configured by hand or set up with the PWE3 control protocol of RFC 4447. The extensions to that control protocol needed to set up and maintain SAToP pseudowires, and the code points allocated for them, are described in separate documents.
sections.plainLanguage: SAToP carries a telephone line across a packet network. It does not look at what is inside the line, so it works for any kind of traffic the line carries, including signalling the provider does not want to interpret. The result is a pseudowire: a circuit that looks continuous to the equipment at each end but is made of packets in between.

sections.title: The Terms the Document Uses
sections.content:
The acronyms come from RFC 3985 and RFC 4197: the customer edge (CE) is the customer device at the end of the circuit, the provider edge (PE) is the provider device that terminates the pseudowire, and the IWF is the interworking function, the block that segments the TDM stream into SAToP packets and, in the other direction, decapsulates the packets and reconstitutes the TDM stream.

Two TDM terms matter for the fault handling. Loss of Signal (LOS) is the condition in which the incoming signal on the TDM attachment circuit cannot be detected, with the entry and exit criteria given in G.775. An Alarm Indication Signal (AIS) is a bit pattern in the TDM stream that says there is an outage upstream. For E1, T1 and E3 circuits the AIS pattern is a run of binary ones of the right length, the all ones pattern, so it can be detected and generated without understanding the framing. The T3 AIS pattern needs T3 framing, so it can only be handled by a structure-aware device.

The four emulated services and their bit rates are E1 at 2048 kbit/s, T1 at 1544 kbit/s (also known as DS1), E3 at 34368 kbit/s, and T3 at 44736 kbit/s (also known as DS3). The protocol does not depend on how the attachment circuit reaches the provider edge: a T1 circuit delivered over copper, multiplexed inside a T3 circuit, carried as a virtual tributary of a SONET or SDH circuit, or delivered over an ATM network with unstructured circuit emulation is treated in the same way. Any carrier layer between the provider edge and the customer edge is terminated by a native service processing device.
sections.plainLanguage: The document uses a few names for the equipment. The customer edge is the device at the customer site, the provider edge is the provider device that terminates the pseudowire, and the interworking function is the part that cuts the stream into packets and puts it back together. The four line types it emulates are E1, T1, E3 and T3.

sections.title: The Packet Format
sections.content:
A SAToP packet has three layers. At the top sit the headers of the packet-switching network and of the pseudowire demultiplexing mechanism. Below them sits the SAToP encapsulation header, which holds the SAToP control word and may also hold a fixed RTP header. At the bottom is the TDM data itself, the payload.

Both UDP and L2TPv3 can provide the pseudowire demultiplexing over an IPv4 or IPv6 packet network, and the MPLS label provides it over an MPLS packet network. The order of the control word and the optional RTP header depends on that choice. With UDP multiplexing the RTP header comes first and the control word follows it, and in every other case the RTP header, when present, immediately follows the control word. The document gives the reason: the arrangement keeps the traditional use of RTP over an IP network with UDP multiplexing, keeps SAToP pseudowires safe on an MPLS network with equal-cost multipath by allowing the packet to be told apart from other traffic on the same label stack, and makes it possible to stitch an L2TPv3 segment to an MPLS segment of the same pseudowire.

The total size of a SAToP packet on a given pseudowire must not exceed the path MTU between the two provider edge devices that terminate it. Implementations that use an IPv4 packet network must mark the IP datagrams they generate as Do Not Fragment.
sections.plainLanguage: Each packet has three parts: the network and demultiplexing headers on top, a small SAToP header in the middle, and the copied telephone bits at the bottom. The network can be IP with UDP or L2TPv3, or MPLS. The middle header holds a 4-byte control word and, if the two ends agreed to use it, an RTP header.

sections.title: The SAToP Control Word
sections.content:
The control word is 4 bytes. Its purpose is to let the far end notice that something is wrong: it detects packet loss and misordering, tells a packet network fault apart from a fault on the customer line, allows invalid data to be left out to save bandwidth, and signals faults detected at the outgoing end back to the incoming end.

Bits 0 to 3 are described in RFC 4385. They must be set to zero unless they are marking the start of an Associated Channel Header, which is needed when the state of the pseudowire is being monitored with Virtual Circuit Connectivity Verification. The L bit marks payload that is invalid because of a fault on the attachment circuit. When it is set the payload may be left out to save bandwidth, and the receiving end must play out the right amount of filler data instead. The document does not fix which TDM faults count as invalidating the data; Loss of Signal and AIS are given as possible examples. Once the fault is repaired the bit must be cleared. The R bit is set by the sending end when the far end has lost a preconfigured number of consecutive packets, and is cleared once the far end has received a preconfigured number of consecutive packets again.

The RSV and FRG bits, which are bits 6 to 9, must be set to zero by the sender and ignored by the receiver. RSV is reserved and FRG marks fragmentation. The LEN field may carry the length of the SAToP packet, that is the header plus the payload, when that length is less than 64 bytes, and must be set to zero otherwise. When LEN is zero the receiver assumes the payload size agreed at setup, and a packet whose actual size does not match is malformed.

The sequence number provides the common pseudowire sequencing function and the detection of lost packets. It follows the rules of RFC 3550 for the RTP sequence number: it is a 16-bit unsigned circular space whose initial value should be random, and it is incremented for each SAToP data packet sent on that pseudowire. A useful property of the layout is that a valid sequence number can always be found in bits 16 to 31 of the first 32-bit word after the demultiplexing header, whatever the packet network or multiplexing method in use, which simplifies implementations that support several encapsulation types and pseudowires made of several segments.
sections.plainLanguage: The control word is 4 bytes and carries the sequence number of the packet, so the far end can tell whether a packet went missing or arrived out of order. Two flag bits matter: one says the payload is invalid because the customer line has a fault, and the other says the far end has lost packets. A length field is used only for short packets.

sections.title: The Payload and How the Bits Are Cut
sections.content:
Every packet of a given pseudowire carries the same number of bytes of TDM data. The payload size is agreed at pseudowire setup, must be the same in both directions, and cannot be changed for the life of the pseudowire. A fixed size lets the receiver know how much data is missing when a packet is lost. The size can be exchanged during setup over the PWE3 control protocol using the Circuit Emulation over Packet or TDM Payload Bytes sub-TLV of the Interface Parameters TLV.

The bytes keep the order they had on the attachment circuit, and consecutive bits fill each byte from the most significant bit to the least significant. Whatever size is chosen, SAToP assumes no alignment to the byte, frame or multiframe structure that TDM framing may impose. All implementations must be able to carry E1 in 256-byte payloads, T1 in 192-byte payloads, and E3 and T3 in 1024-byte payloads. Payload sizes that are multiples of 47 bytes may be used with unstructured ATM circuit emulation.

One special mode exists for T1 lines that are already padded to a whole number of bytes, which happens when the T1 is taken out of a SONET or SDH virtual tributary or when a dual-mode E1 and T1 framer removes the framing. In this octet-aligned T1 mode the payload is a number of 25-byte subframes, each carrying 193 bits of TDM data and 7 bits of padding. Support is optional, and an octet-aligned T1 pseudowire is not interoperable with a T1 pseudowire carrying an unaligned bit-stream. Implementations that support the mode must be able to carry a 200-byte payload, that is eight subframes, which is exactly 1 millisecond of TDM data. The mode also allows the packetization delay to be chosen as any whole multiple of 125 microseconds.
sections.plainLanguage: Each packet holds the same number of bits from the line, and the size is fixed when the circuit is set up, so the receiver always knows how much is missing when a packet is lost. The bits are copied across in the order they arrive, with no regard for the framing structure of the line. For T1 lines that are already a whole number of bytes, a special mode groups the bits into 25-byte subframes.

sections.title: How the Two Ends Behave
sections.content:
Emulating a circuit edge to edge needs both attachment circuits to be of the same type, and the service type is exchanged at pseudowire setup. In the direction towards the packet network, the interworking function packetizes the TDM data using the agreed number of payload bytes, inserts the sequence numbers, flags and timestamps if the RTP header is used, prepends the SAToP, demultiplexing and network headers, and transmits the packets.

In the direction towards the customer edge, the interworking function should keep a jitter buffer, holding the payload of received packets before playing it out to the local circuit, and the buffer size should be configurable so it can absorb the delay variation of the particular packet network. It should use the control word sequence number to detect lost and misordered packets, and it may reorder misordered packets, discarding any it cannot reorder and treating them as lost. The payload of a packet marked with the L bit should be replaced by the equivalent amount of the all ones pattern even when it was not omitted, and the payload of every lost packet must be replaced with replacement data whose contents are implementation-specific and locally configurable, with the all ones pattern as the required default.

Before the pseudowire is set up, and after it is torn down, the interworking function must play out the all ones pattern. Once the pseudowire is set up, it stores received payloads in the jitter buffer but still plays out the all ones pattern until a preconfigured amount of TDM data has been received in consecutive packets, usually half the jitter buffer, or until an intermediate state timer expires. It then enters normal operation, where it recovers the clock, plays out the jitter buffer against that clock, and may monitor defects and collect performance data. If a preconfigured number of consecutive packets is lost, or the timer expires too early, it enters the packet loss state, in which the far end should set the R bit on every packet it sends. Leaving that state needs a preconfigured number of consecutive valid packets, and successfully reordered packets count towards it.

Besides the packet loss state, the receiving end may detect stray packets, malformed packets, an excessive packet loss rate, a buffer overrun and remote packet loss. Malformed packets are found by comparing the expected packet size, taking the L bit into account, with the size inferred from the demultiplexing headers, and, when RTP is used, by checking the payload type against the value allocated for that direction. Each defect has a state, a detection criterion that moves the device out of normal operation, and an alarm that may be reported to the management system. Alarms are reported only when the defect persists for a preconfigured time, typically 2.5 seconds, and are cleared after the defect has been absent for another preconfigured time, typically 10 seconds. Stray packets must be discarded and must not affect the packet loss detection. The interworking function must also give the customer edge an indication of whether the TDM data is valid, either by transporting or by generating the native AIS, which for T3 needs a structure-aware device.
sections.plainLanguage: The sending end copies the line into packets and puts the headers on. The receiving end holds the arriving packets in a buffer, plays them out on the recovered clock, and fills any gap with the all ones pattern so the customer line keeps running. When packets are lost for long enough the receiving end says so by setting a flag that the sender copies into every packet. A loss of signal on the customer line is passed on the same way.

sections.title: Quality of Service, Congestion and Monitoring
sections.content:
SAToP should use the quality of service mechanisms of the packet network underneath it. On a network with Diffserv and a per-domain behaviour that guarantees low jitter and low loss, the pseudowire should use that behaviour within the admission and allocation rules the network applies. On an Intserv network, Guaranteed Service with the right bandwidth reservation should be used, so the reservation covers the aggregate TDM traffic.

SAToP pseudowires are inelastic constant bit-rate flows. They cannot respond to congestion in the TCP-friendly way of RFC 2914, although the share of bandwidth they take stays constant. Unchecked demand can therefore add to congestion in the network and disturb network control protocols. The document recommends carrying SAToP pseudowires across traffic-engineered networks that provide bandwidth reservation with admission control, or forwarding priority with boundary traffic conditioning. IntServ domains with Guaranteed Service and Diffserv domains with Expedited Forwarding are given as examples. To help with boundary conditioning, SAToP packets should not use the Diffserv code point reserved for the default per-hop behaviour.

On a best-effort network, a pseudowire should watch its packet loss to detect severe congestion, and on detecting it should shut down in both directions for a time. The document does not define the criteria for severe congestion or the shutdown method, and leaves that for further study, but offers three guidelines. The performance monitoring definitions give entry and exit criteria for the unavailable state that match the unavailable state of the emulated circuit in G.826, which lowers the risk of shutting down a circuit the customer still considers available. Where the pseudowire was set up with the PWE3 control protocol or with L2TPv3, the regular teardown procedures of those protocols should be used. And if one end stops sending for long enough, the other end sees total packet loss, detects severe congestion and stops sending too, which achieves a shutdown in both directions.

Performance monitoring for the pseudowire is optional and only starts once the receiving end has left its intermediate state. The document defines an error event as the insertion of one replacement packet into the jitter buffer, an errored data block as a block of data played out to the circuit, sized by the G.826 rules, that contains at least one error event, and a defect as the packet loss state of the receiving end. The errored, severely errored and unavailable seconds parameters are then derived from those definitions following G.826.
sections.plainLanguage: SAToP takes a fixed slice of bandwidth and cannot slow down when the network is busy, so it should run on a network that reserves bandwidth or gives it priority. On a best-effort network it should watch for heavy packet loss and, if it sees it, stop the circuit in both directions for a while so the rest of the network can recover. The document also defines how to count errors for maintenance reports.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
SAToP neither improves nor worsens the security of the packet network underneath it. It relies on that network for encryption, integrity and authentication whenever those are required. A SAToP pseudowire shares the exposure of any other pseudowire to attacks at that layer, and uses whatever mechanisms are developed for pseudowires generally; those methods are outside the scope of this document.

Where the optional RTP header is used to carry timing information, SRTP as described in RFC 3711 is not recommended as a replacement for protection at the pseudowire layer. Two properties of SAToP do help. Its ability to detect a misconnection makes it more resilient to misconfiguration and to some kinds of denial-of-service attack. And because the sequence numbers in the control word and in the optional RTP header start from a random value, known-plaintext attacks on an encrypted pseudowire become harder. Encryption of pseudowires is itself outside the scope of the document.

The applicability statement notes what SAToP does and does not give the operator. It carries the stream in its entirety, including any signalling inside it, which means the emulated services are sensitive to packet loss in the packet network, and while careful replacement data can keep the customer interface up through occasional loss, other effects of loss, such as errored blocks, cannot be prevented. The packetization delay, the delay of the packet network and the delay of the jitter buffer all add to the end-to-end delay, so both delay and delay variation should be estimated before the pseudowire is set up. SAToP gives no protection against an outage of the packet network, although loss replacement and reordering make the emulated service more tolerant of a fast reroute. Structure-aware emulation hides the effect of packet loss entirely, because framing and the cyclic redundancy checks are generated locally, but that is a different mechanism and outside this document.
sections.plainLanguage: SAToP adds no security of its own. Encryption, integrity and authentication come from the packet network or from the protections that apply to pseudowires in general. Two details help a little: the protocol can notice when the two ends are wired to the wrong circuit, and it starts its sequence numbers at a random value, which makes guessing harder.

fields.desc: Set when the payload is invalid because of an attachment circuit fault.

fields.desc: Set by the sending end when the far end has lost consecutive packets.

fields.desc: Reserved; set to zero by the sender and ignored by the receiver.

fields.desc: Length of the packet in bytes when it is less than 64, otherwise zero.

fields.name: Sequence Number
fields.desc: 16-bit circular counter, incremented for every data packet sent.
